newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Russia says ball in NATO's court on security deal.
newsitem.headline: Russia says ball in NATO's court on security deal.

text.p: Russia and NATO have resolved most of the problems blocking agreement on a post-Cold War partnerhip and progress now depends on the Western alliance, a Russian foreign ministry source told Interfax news agency on Monday.

The source said differences remained on military matters and that the onus was on NATO Secretary General Javier Solana to make a breakthrough in his talks with Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov in Luxembourg on Tuesday.

"It depends entirely on NATO if the meeting in Luxembourg on May 6 is to be the last before the signing of the document on relations between Russia and the North Atlantic alliance," Interfax said, quoting a "senior foreign ministry source".

Russia opposes NATO's plans to offer membership to some former members of the now defunct Moscow-led Warsaw Pact at a summit in Madrid in July. Poland, the Czech Republic and Hungary are at the head of the queue to join.

But President Boris Yeltsin, realising NATO expansion is going ahead with or without Russian consent, wants an agreement mapping a new relationship between Russia and the North Atlantic Treaty Organisation to be signed on May 27 in Paris.
NATO officials say a deal may be possible by then but it is not certain that all differences can be narrowed in time.

U.S. and Russian officials said progress was made at talks in Moscow last week between Primakov and U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, but NATO has given no clues about when an accord might be signed.
"The Russian side has shown its negotiating partners its cards and NATO has shown its cards," the Russian foreign ministry source told Interfax.
"In the last four rounds of negotiations between Primakov and Solana, three of which were in Moscow and one in Brussels, most questions have been agreed."
But the source said Moscow was sticking to demands for a clear, binding agreement on military matters.

"The Russian side insists everything here is utterly clear and concrete. NATO would like to get off with passionate declarations saying they have no plans, or intentions or reasons, let's say, for stationing nuclear weapons on the territory of new member states of this bloc," the official said.
He added: "An assertion has any sense only if it is set out in a legally binding document.
Yeltsin seemed to drop demands for a legally binding treaty at a Russia-U.S. summit in Helsinki in March but wants any accord to be signed by him and NATO heads of state or government.
Western officials say the agreement would set up a joint council with Russia, giving Moscow a voice in important decisions affecting its security interests in Europe.

Russia wants binding guarantees from NATO that it will not move nuclear or conventional forces into the territory of the new members. NATO says it has no plans to put nuclear arms or "substantial" conventional forces on new members' territory, but is reluctant to be tied down legally.
Another problem is the inconclusive state of talks in Vienna on amending the 1990 Conventional Forces in Europe (CFE) treaty limiting the numbers of weapons and where they can be placed.

NATO wants to scrap group ceilings for force levels in favour of purely national ceilings, but Russia wants to retain them. NATO demands the right to station some foreign forces in other countries but Russia rejects this.
Russia wants the agreement with NATO to mention a future CFE accord because that would be a firmer commitment.
